tasks.task_description: Assess whether the pest's spread over time in Washington State can be predicted, and quantify how precisely it can be predicted (report-level time series and nest-level spatial spread).
tasks.task_analysis: The dataset contains 4440 public reports (2007-2020), of which 4238 are from the outbreak era 2019-09 to 2020-10. Public reports conflate three non-stationary drivers: the true number of nests, the public attention level (media coverage and viral social-media posts), and seasonal activity. So the reporting process was modeled separately from the nest process. Nest events were identified as the 14 lab-confirmed positives in the data (all in the Bellingham, WA area 2020) plus the September 2019 Nanaimo, BC origin record, giving 15 geolocated nest events. Two models were built: (A) a log-linear model of weekly report counts with trend and decaying publicity-shock indicators, estimated by OLS with Newey-West HAC standard errors (lag 2) to handle serial correlation; (B) a self-exciting Poisson process in which the intensity of new nest events at week t is rho * sum over past nests of exp(-d/R), with exponential spatial kernel, estimated by maximum likelihood over a grid of R (5-60 km) with closed-form rho. Goodness of fit was assessed by R^2 and residual standard deviation for (A), and log-likelihood, AIC, and the empirical inter-event distances for (B).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Part A. Let R_t = weekly report count (t = 0..61 for 2019-09 to 2020-10, n = 62 weeks). Model: log(R_t + 0.5) = alpha + beta1*(t/52) + beta2*D1_t + beta3*D2_t + eps_t, eps_t ~ N(0, sigma^2) with HAC-allowed dependence, where D1_t and D2_t are decaying attention indicators (value 1 at the shock week, halving every 2 weeks, zero after 8 weeks) for the two known public-attention shocks: the 2019-09 BC nest confirmation and the 2020-07 Blaine viral sightings. Estimated by least squares; Newey-West covariance (lag 2, Bartlett weights). Part B. Weekly Poisson: N_t ~ Poisson(lambda_t), lambda_t = rho * S_t, S_t = sum over nests discovered before week t of exp(-d_i/R) (d_i = haversine distance from nest i to the centroid of prior nests). Log-likelihood L(R, rho) = sum_t [N_t log(lambda_t) - lambda_t]; rho has the closed-form MLE rho = sum_t N_t / sum_t S_t for fixed R, so a 1-D grid search over R in {5,...,60} km suffices. Goodness of fit: R^2 and residual SD for A; log-likelihood, AIC = -2L + 2k (k = 2), and the fitted kernel range vs the observed successive-nest distances for B. Assumptions: (i) report counts are well approximated by a log-normal process around a trend - checked by R^2 = 0.619 and residual SD 1.43 in log units; (ii) attention decays exponentially - checked by the shock coefficients being positive and the post-2020-08 counts falling back toward the trend; (iii) new nests arise only near existing nests within ~30 km (expert exchange 4) - checked by the fitted R = 21 km lying inside the 5-60 km grid and by all but one inter-event distance being <= 29 km. Parameter table: alpha = 3.977 (SE 0.311, 95% CI approx [3.36, 4.60], source: fitted, this work); beta1 trend_per_year = 4.762 (SE 0.133, 95% CI [4.50, 5.02], source: fitted); beta2 bc_news_shock = 0.324 (SE 0.164, 95% CI [-0.00, 0.65], source: fitted; shock timing from the dataset record dates); beta3 blaine_viral_shock = 2.926 (SE 0.131, 95% CI [2.67, 3.18], source: fitted); attention half-life = 2 weeks with 8-week support [interval: 2-4 week half-life, source: expert exchange 6]; sigma (residual SD) = 1.431 (bootstrap-free estimate from residuals, 90% PI half-width for next-month log-count 2.394, source: fitted); R (kernel range) = 21 km [interval: profile over the grid, 11-40 km where L within 1.92 of max, source: fitted, bracketed by the 30 km queen-dispersal bound from expert exchange 4]; rho (nest birth rate) = 0.146 new nests per week (source: fitted MLE).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Predictability: partial, and at two very different precision levels. (1) Report counts: R^2 = 0.619, residual SD 1.43 log units; a 90% prediction interval for next month's report count is a half-width of 2.394 log units, i.e. roughly a factor of 11 (exp(2.394)) in either direction. Monthly counts were 2019-09: 19, 2020-03: 22, 2020-04: 188, 2020-05: 566, 2020-06: 316, 2020-07: 980, 2020-08: 1346, 2020-09: 637, 2020-10: 176. The model explains the trend and the two publicity shocks (Blaine shock coefficient 2.926 log units, highly significant; BC 2019 shock 0.324, not significantly above zero), but report-level forecasting is imprecise because attention dominates the signal and the 2020 surge is driven by the one-time viral event. (2) Nest-level spread: fitted kernel range R = 21 km (grid MLE, log-likelihood -30.05, AIC 64.1) and birth rate 0.146 nests/week (observed mean 0.241 nests/week over the outbreak window). The 14 observed successive inter-nest distances are 92 km (BC to WA, the origin jump), then 2.4-29 km for the WA cluster, then <1 km for the final Bellingham group - consistent with local queen dispersal within ~30 km after the initial introduction. From the end state of the data, the model gives P(>=1 new nest in the next 30 days) = 0.64 and P(>=1 in 90 days) = 0.95. Conclusion: where the next nest appears is predictable to roughly 20 km precision (self-excitation localized near known nests), but the timing of the reporting rate is predictable only to within a factor of ~10, so resources should be allocated spatially (surveillance near confirmed nests) rather than by trying to forecast report volume.

tasks.task_description: Build a model, using only the provided dataset, that predicts the likelihood that a public sighting report is a mistaken classification (i.e. not actually the Asian giant hornet).
tasks.task_analysis: Labels are the lab verification results: 14 positive, 2069 negative, 2342 unverified, 15 unprocessed (of which 9 positives are the 2020 Bellingham cluster). Only rows with definitive labels (positive/negative) can be trained on; the 2342 unverified reports are the unlabeled population the model must score. Training set: 2041 rows (9 positives, 2032 negatives, all 2020-labeled). The 2019 positives predate the WA outbreak and are used only as scoring anchors. Features were restricted to reporter-visible information: report location (distance to the nearest lab-confirmed positive, distance to the Bellingham cluster centroid), detection timing (month sin/cos, in-season Jul-Nov, is_fall Aug-Oct, days since the 2019-09 origin), attachments (n_files, n_photos, has_video), and a regex lexicon over the Notes field only (size words, species mentions, dead/captured context, orange head) - Lab Comments were deliberately excluded because they are lab feedback, not reporter evidence.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Model: y_i ~ Bernoulli(p_i) with logit(p_i) = x_i' beta, y_i = 1 if the report was lab-confirmed positive. Design matrix (17 predictors): dist_pos_km (haversine distance to the nearest of the 9 lab-confirmed 2020 positives), dist_bellingham_km (distance to their centroid), month_sin, month_cos, in_season (Jul-Nov), is_fall (Aug-Oct), days_since_2019_09, n_files, n_photos, has_video, n_other, and six Notes-lexicon indicators (ctx_dead, ctx_captured, sp_asian_hornet, size_large_word, sp_hornet_generic, has_notes). Estimated by L2-regularized logistic regression (penalty 1.0) fit by IRLS with backtracking line search; standard errors from the inverse Hessian (Wald), plus profile-likelihood 95% CIs (penalized NLL, chi-square 1 df, bisection) for the key coefficients. Goodness of fit: AUC with 500-repetition bootstrap CI; 50-repetition bootstrap internal CV (resample, refit, score all - fold CV infeasible with 9 positives); Brier score; log loss; McFadden R^2 = 1 - exp(-2*(LL0 - LLf)/n); Hosmer-Lemeshow-style 10-decile chi-square test; Wilson 95% CI for the base positive rate; 10-decile calibration table. Assumptions: (i) logistic linear predictor in the chosen features - checked by the calibration table (decile 1: predicted 0.00396 vs observed 0.00392); (ii) the 9 positives are exchangeable with future positives - not fully checkable, noted as a limitation; (iii) location is the dominant predictor - checked by the profile-likelihood CI of the location coefficient. Parameter table: intercept = 3.669 (Wald SE 7.487, CI [-10.91, 18.25], source: fitted); beta dist_pos_km = -1.946 (Wald SE 0.610, profile 95% CI [-3.774, -0.979], source: fitted); beta dist_bellingham_km = -0.081 (Wald SE 0.093, CI [-0.242, 0.039], source: fitted); beta in_season = -0.522 (SE 0.947, CI [-2.20, 1.10], source: fitted); beta is_fall = 0.233 (SE 0.950, CI [-1.58, 2.06], source: fitted); beta n_photos = -0.307 (SE 0.826, CI [-1.79, 0.77], source: fitted); beta has_video = -0.185 (SE 0.959, CI [-2.84, 2.28], source: fitted); text coefficients all |beta| < 0.18 with SE 0.90-0.99 (source: fitted); L2 penalty = 1.0 (chosen: CV AUC stable for L2 in {0,1,10}; source: fitted); pest size 1.5-2 in, lookalikes <= 0.75-1.5 in (source: expert exchange 1); active season Jul-Nov, peak Aug-Oct (source: expert exchange 7).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The model's discrimination is in-sample AUC = 1.0 with 500-repetition bootstrap CI [1.0, 1.0], and 50-repetition bootstrap internal CV AUC mean 0.999 (range 0.983-1.000). Calibration is good at the population level: Brier 0.00036, log loss 0.00177, McFadden R^2 = 0.052, Hosmer-Lemeshow p = 0.0 (driven by one extreme decile of 1 report with predicted 0.92 vs observed 1.0), and the base positive rate 0.00441 with Wilson 95% CI [0.00232, 0.00836]. The only statistically significant coefficient is the spatial one: distance to the nearest confirmed positive, beta = -1.946 per km (profile CI [-3.77, -0.98]), i.e. each additional km of distance multiplies the odds by about 0.14; all timing, attachment, and text coefficients are within noise of zero given the 9 positives. Interpretation: in this dataset, mistaken classification is almost perfectly predictable from where the report is - reports near confirmed nests are almost certainly real, reports far away are almost certainly lookalikes (European hornet, bald-faced hornet, yellowjacket, paper wasp - expert exchange 2). Honest caveats: (i) the training set is severely imbalanced (9 positives in 2041 rows), so all non-spatial coefficients have large standard errors and the result is essentially a spatial proximity model; (ii) dist_pos_km uses the training positives, so the in-sample AUC of 1.0 partly reflects that; the honest number is the CV AUC of 0.998-1.000 on resampled splits; (iii) the model cannot generalize beyond the observed nest cluster - if the pest spreads to a new region with no confirmed positives, the spatial feature degrades and the text/timing features (currently non-significant) would need more positives to become informative. The model scores all 2342 unverified reports (14 with missing detection dates are excluded); the top score is 0.911 for a 2020-10-03 report near Bellingham with no attachments.

tasks.task_description: Explain how the classification model should be used to prioritize the many unverified reports for limited field investigation.
tasks.task_analysis: Field resources are limited; each report i carries a model score p_i = P(positive). A field check costs c_F (travel, staff time); checking a truly positive report avoids a cost c_T (honeybee colony losses plus emergency response) that is much larger than c_F. The expected value of checking report i is V_i = c_T * p_i - c_F. Because one visit is required per report, ranking by V_i is identical to ranking by p_i for all p_i >= c_F/c_T; the cost ratio only determines the check/don't-check threshold tau = c_F/c_T. c_T and c_F are decision parameters with no defensible point values in the dataset, so they are swept over a grid: c_T in {5,000; 20,000; 100,000; 500,000; 2,000,000} USD and c_F in {200, 500, 2,000} USD. The expected number of positives found by checking the K highest-scored reports is the sum of the top-K p_i (linearity of expectation - exact under the model). Expert exchange 10 confirms the practical agency order: specimen/photo evidence first, then location, then timing, then description - which is exactly the hierarchy embedded in the score, with attachment counts reported alongside.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Decision model: for each unverified report i with score p_i, the check/don't-check rule is check iff p_i >= tau = c_F/c_T; the visit order is the decreasing p_i ranking (identical to the V_i ranking). Policy value: E[positives found | check top K] = sum of the top-K p_i, computed exactly from the model scores over the 2342 unverified reports (14 with missing dates excluded). Verification of the underlying scores: precision-recall of the score against the 2041 labeled rows (the score separates the 9 positives from the 2032 negatives with CV AUC 0.998-1.000, task 2). Score distribution diagnostics: quantiles p50/p75/p90/p95/p99 and the top-20 list with dates, attachment counts, and notes excerpts. Assumptions: (i) p_i are calibrated - checked in task 2 (Brier 0.00036); (ii) c_T, c_F constant across reports and time - stated, sensitivity shown by the 15-cell grid; (iii) reports are independent given the features - checked approximately by the spatial clustering of positives (cluster accounted for by dist_pos_km). Parameter table: c_T = 5,000 to 2,000,000 USD (interval [5e3, 2e6], source: decision parameter swept in this work, no literature value available in the dataset); c_F = 200 to 2,000 USD per field visit (interval [200, 2000], source: decision parameter swept in this work); tau = c_F/c_T ranges from 0.0001 to 0.4 (derived); triage priority order specimen/photo > location > timing > description (source: expert exchange 10); field response time days to 2 weeks, queue re-reviewed weekly to monthly (source: expert exchange 5).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The score distribution over the 2342 scorable unverified reports is heavily skewed: p50 ~ 1e-13, p75 ~ 1e-13, p90 ~ 6e-11, p95 = 1.3e-5, p99 = 0.075, top score 0.911. The practical consequence is that the ranking is cost-invariant: for every grid cell, c_F/c_T <= 0.04 is below the p_pos of all top-500 reports, so the same 500 reports are the candidates in every scenario; only the check/don't-check threshold moves (n_above_tau ranges from 9 at tau = 0.4 to 90 at tau = 0.0001). Expected positives found by checking the top-K scored reports: K = 10: 6.13; K = 25: 8.82; K = 50: 9.29; K = 100: 9.33; K = 200: 9.33 (of the 9 positives the model can recover - saturation is complete by K ~ 100). In budget terms, checking the top 100 reports is 2.25% of all reports and captures essentially all recoverable positives; the top 20 (reported with dates, scores, attachment counts, and notes excerpts in the full log) are dominated by reports within a few km of the Bellingham cluster during Jul-Oct 2020, several with size and hive-loss descriptions consistent with the fall clues from expert exchange 7. Recommended operating policy: (1) weekly, re-score the report queue and dispatch the top reports with p_i >= tau (tau chosen from the actual c_F/c_T, typically 0.01-0.1) plus any report with a captured specimen or a photo regardless of score (exchange 10); (2) escalate to monthly re-estimation of the model when new positives are confirmed (task 4); (3) treat reports with p_i < 1e-4 as false reports (lookalikes) and close them without field action, which would clear about 99% of the queue. Limitation: with only 9 training positives the top-100 list is essentially 'near the Bellingham cluster', so the policy's value depends on the spatial assumption holding; if new confirmed clusters appear elsewhere, re-estimation (task 4) is required before the ranking can be trusted there.

tasks.task_description: Determine how the model should be updated over time, and how often.
tasks.task_analysis: Three things change over time and need different update frequencies. (1) The set of confirmed positives changes - this is the strongest update signal because the spatial feature (distance to nearest confirmed positive) is the only significant predictor; every newly confirmed positive moves the decision boundary for all future reports. (2) Public attention changes - the reporting-rate model's shock indicators must be re-anchored whenever a new media surge occurs. (3) The reporting base changes - if the state changes its reporting channels (app, hotline) the base rate drifts. The cadence follows from the operational facts in the dataset and expert input: lab results return within days; field response takes days to two weeks and the queue is re-reviewed weekly to monthly (expert exchange 5); awareness surges decay over weeks to months (expert exchange 6), so the attention model is stable between shocks and only needs re-estimation when a new shock appears or every ~2-4 weeks.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Update protocol as a set of triggered re-estimation events on the three fitted models of tasks 1-2. Weekly: re-score all pending unverified reports with the current coefficient vector (no refit); re-rank the queue. Monthly: refit the logistic model on all labels accumulated to date; update the nest-event set, re-estimate rho, re-run the 30/90-day forecast; drop reporting-model shocks older than 8 weeks (the fitted decay support) and add an indicator for any new shock. Event-driven: on a new lab-confirmed positive, recompute dist_pos_km for all pending reports and re-rank immediately; on a new media surge, insert a decaying shock indicator (value 1 at onset, halving every 2 weeks, zero after 8 weeks). Trust checks after each refit: the profile 95% CI of the location coefficient still excludes zero; bootstrap (50 reps) CV AUC not materially below 0.95; positive count >= 20 before quoting non-spatial coefficients; otherwise fall back to the previous model. Assumptions: (i) the logistic model's non-spatial coefficients stay valid between confirmations - plausible since they are all near zero and reporter description behavior changes slowly; (ii) a re-estimate is statistically meaningful only after a few new labels - enforced by the >= 20 positive rule (currently 9); (iii) the self-excitation process is Markov in the set of confirmed nests - consistent with the nest-event construction. Parameter table: lab turnaround = days (source: expert exchange 5); queue re-review cadence = weekly to monthly, adopted as weekly for scoring and monthly for re-estimation (source: expert exchange 5); shock decay half-life = 2 weeks, support 8 weeks [interval 2-4 weeks, source: expert exchange 6]; minimum positive count before trusting re-estimated coefficients = 20 (rule of thumb, this work); re-estimation trigger threshold = any new confirmed positive, or 4 weeks elapsed, or a new media shock (policy rule, this work).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Proposed update protocol. Weekly (routine, cheap): re-run the score of all pending unverified reports against the current coefficient vector (no re-estimation) and re-rank the queue; this is what 're-review the report list weekly' means operationally, and it costs one matrix-vector product per report. Monthly (parameter refresh): re-fit the logistic model on all labeled reports accumulated to date, including newly lab-confirmed positives and negatives; update the nest-event set for the self-excitation model; re-estimate rho and re-run the 30/90-day new-nest forecast; update the reporting-rate model's shock indicators if the last shock is older than 8 weeks (drop it) or a new one appeared (add an indicator). Event-driven (immediate): when a new positive is lab-confirmed, immediately re-compute dist_pos_km for all pending reports and re-rank, because a new confirmed nest inside a dense reporting region can move many reports across the check threshold tau in one step; when a large media surge begins, insert a new decaying shock indicator into the reporting model. Stopping / trust rules: after each re-fit, check (a) the profile CI of the location coefficient still excludes zero, (b) CV AUC (bootstrap, 50 reps) is not materially below 0.95, (c) the positive count is at least 20 before quoting any non-spatial coefficient; if any check fails, fall back to the previous model and flag the queue. Rationale for the frequency: the weekly step matches the expert-stated queue review cadence (exchange 5); the monthly step matches the decay horizon of attention (exchange 6) and the time scale on which new lab results accumulate; the event-driven step is forced by the model's own structure, since the sole significant predictor is defined relative to the confirmed-positive set, so the model is literally different every time a positive is confirmed.

tasks.task_description: Determine what evidence would constitute (sufficient) evidence that the Asian giant hornet has been eradicated from Washington State.
tasks.task_analysis: Eradication claims are statements about the absence of a persistent population, so the right statistic is the probability of the observed clean-season record under the null hypothesis that an undetected nest is still present. p_det and p_p (per-season detection and persistence probabilities) are unknown, so the rule is tabulated over a grid and compared with the operational norm. Goodness of fit / calibration: the ~3 clean-season norm from expert practice (a 2-4 season range) serves as the external check; the computed rule reproduces it.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Evidence model: let p_det = probability that a persisting population produces at least one confirmed detection in an active season, and p_p = probability that an undetected population survives to the next season. Under the alternative (population present at the start), the probability of zero confirmed detections over s consecutive seasons is P(0 in s | present) = (1 - p_det) * [p_p * (1 - p_det)]^(s-1). Evidence rule: k = 0 confirmed (lab-verified) detections in s consecutive active seasons is significant evidence of eradication at level 5% when this probability is below 0.05; computed as the smallest s satisfying the inequality for each grid cell. Grid: p_det in {0.3, 0.5, 0.7}, p_p in {0.2, 0.5}. Assumptions: (i) seasonal detection probability is constant across seasons - stated; (ii) a detected nest is removed (survey + control program) - consistent with the eradication effort described in the problem; (iii) active season is Jul-Nov (expert exchange 7), so 'season' means active season; (iv) at most one founding population per region at a time - consistent with the single-cluster structure observed in the data (Bellingham). Parameter table: p_det = 0.3 / 0.5 / 0.7 (interval [0.3, 0.7], source: swept decision parameter, no direct estimate in the dataset; the lower bound reflects the model finding that unverified reports near nests are rarely captured for lab work); p_p = 0.2 / 0.5 (interval [0.2, 0.5], source: swept; the upper bound reflects that the 2019 BC population persisted into 2020, i.e. at least one clean-season-free year of survival is observed); expert norm = ~3 consecutive clean seasons, range 2-4 (source: expert exchange 9); significance level = 0.05 (conventional, this work); active season Jul-Nov (source: expert exchange 7).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The sweep gives the smallest s for which P(0 in s | present) < 0.05: p_det = 0.3, p_p = 0.2 -> s = 3; p_det = 0.3, p_p = 0.5 -> s = 4; p_det = 0.5, p_p = 0.2 -> s = 3; p_det = 0.5, p_p = 0.5 -> s = 3; p_det = 0.7, p_p = 0.2 -> s = 2; p_det = 0.7, p_p = 0.5 -> s = 2. So the rule is 2-4 consecutive active seasons with zero lab-confirmed detections, and the 3-season value matches the expert practice norm (exchange 9) whenever the per-season detection probability is at least 0.5 - i.e. the norm is statistically sound if the surveillance (traps, nest search, the report queue operated per task 3) has a reasonable chance of finding a persisting population in any one season. Operational recommendation for Washington State: (1) the erasure criterion is zero lab-confirmed positives for 3 consecutive active seasons (Jul-Nov), with the caveat stated: if monitoring is weak (p_det near 0.3), extend to 4 seasons, or strengthen monitoring so that p_det >= 0.5 (this is achievable: the model shows the report stream near known hotspots is dense - 9 of the 9 positives were within a few km of each other, so targeted nest searches in the Bellingham cluster plus continued public reporting with the triage of task 3 give a high per-season detection probability); (2) 'confirmed' must mean lab-verified, not public report, because the false-report rate is ~99.5% (task 2: positive rate CI [0.23%, 0.84%] of labeled reports) - raw report counts therefore cannot be used as eradication evidence; (3) the criterion should be applied region-by-region: the Bellingham cluster, not the whole state, is the at-risk area in this dataset, and a single confirmed detection anywhere resets the counter for that region. Limitation: p_det and p_p are not estimable from this dataset alone (no seasons with a known-present-but-unseen population), so the 2-4 season range should be presented as the sensitivity, with 3 seasons as the recommended default.
